title: Leadership From the Ground Up
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note uses the late Napa winemaker Tom Rinaldi, who worked 50 harvests and founded the winemaking at Duckhorn Vineyards, to argue that leaders should stand where the work happens. Rinaldi sampled grapes in the vineyard, walked the cellar barrel by barrel and built every blend himself, because a lab report gives the summary while tasting gives the differences. The piece contrasts leaders who judge operations from dashboards with those who close the distance between decision and work. It adds that leaders earn the right to use judgment only after mastering the fundamentals, and that a formula is a decision someone made for a different season. The three lessons are to get close to the work, master the rules, and then trust judgment over formula.
points: Leaders who judge from dashboards learn the summary, while leaders who stand where the work happens learn the differences where quality lives.
Closing the distance between the decision and the work gives a leader's calls a credibility that no title can provide.
Judgment has to be earned by first learning the fundamentals, and then leaders owe their organization both rules and judgment.
A formula is a decision someone made for a different season, so leaders must adapt rather than replicate.
The measure of leadership from the ground up is that the work gets better, and so do the people who will do it next.
quotes: Leaders who judge their operations from dashboards learn the summary. Leaders who stand where the work happens learn the differences. Tom Rinaldi believed the differences are where quality lives.
A lab report can tell a winemaker the sugar level in a block of grapes. Only tasting the fruit tells them whether it is ready to pick.
Rinaldi spent his career closing the distance between the decision and the work. That habit gave his calls a credibility no title could provide.
Wines have seasons, he explained. The same Cabernet grape on a hilltop and on a valley floor will yield two different personalities. A formula is a decision someone made for a different season.
Rinaldi believed leaders earn the right to use judgment by first learning the fundamentals. Then they owe it to their organization to use both.

Get close to the work because you cannot discern what you have not tasted. Master the rules because judgment without fundamentals is guesswork. Then trust judgment over formula because no two seasons are alike.
That is the measure of leadership from the ground up. The work gets better, and so do the people who will do it next.
